title: Your DMs Are a Lead Inbox. Here's How to Answer Every One While You Work
summary: How an AI DM agent answers Instagram/Facebook messages within minutes, qualifies prospects and books calls on your calendar, so late-night and weekend inquiries stop going cold.

post.title: Your DMs Are a Lead Inbox. Here's How to Answer Every One While You Work
post.metaDescription: People message your business on Instagram and Facebook at all hours. Here's how an AI DM agent answers in minutes, qualifies them, and books the call for you.
intro: It's 9:40 on a Tuesday night. You're finally off your feet when someone sends your business page a message: "Hey, do you have anything open this week? How much is it?" You see the notification, tell yourself you'll answer first thing in the morning, and put the phone down.

By morning there's a second message under it, "Never mind, found someone," or, more likely, nothing at all. They didn't wait. They messaged three businesses, and whoever answered first got the booking.

That message wasn't a social media chore. It was a lead with their hand up, asking to buy. If your DMs only get answered when you have a free minute, you're losing clients you already paid to attract. Here's what actually fixes it.

sections.heading: Why the first reply wins
paragraphs: People who message a business are rarely loyal to that business yet. They're comparing. The question they're really asking is "who will take care of this for me, soon?", and the first business that answers clearly gets the conversation.

This isn't a new idea. A Harvard Business Review study of about 1.25 million leads across 42 companies found that businesses who responded within an hour were roughly seven times more likely to qualify the lead than those who waited even one more hour. Meanwhile, Sprout Social's data puts the average business response time on social at around five hours.

Five hours is a long time for someone who's ready to book. For you, it usually isn't laziness. You're with a client, on a job, driving, or asleep. The gap between when the message arrives and when you can answer is where the lead goes cold.

sections.heading: What an AI DM agent actually does for you
paragraphs: An AI DM agent sits on your Instagram and Facebook inbox and answers every message within a minute or two, day or night. Not with a canned "Thanks, we'll get back to you!" but with a real reply in your voice that moves the conversation forward.
In practice, the agent handles the same three things you would if you had the time:
1. It answers the question. Price ranges, hours, location, what's included, whether you handle their specific problem. It works from the facts you give it, so it doesn't make things up.
2. It asks one or two qualifying questions. What they need, when, and whether they're local. That's enough to tell a real prospect from someone just browsing.
3. It offers times and books the call or appointment directly on your calendar, then sends the confirmation. You find out when it shows up in your schedule.
When something needs you personally, like an unusual request, a complaint, or a question it isn't sure about, it hands the thread to you instead of guessing.

sections.heading: What changes in your week
paragraphs: The biggest change is that you stop doing triage from your phone. You're not half-listening to a client while drafting a reply in your head, and you're not answering DMs at 11pm to keep up.

Your calendar fills from conversations that would have died overnight. The late-evening and weekend messages, which are often the ones from people who are most ready to act, get answered while they're still on the app.

You also get a clearer picture of demand. Every conversation is logged, so you can see how many people asked about price, how many booked, and where people drop off. That tells you whether the problem is your offer, your price, or simply follow-up.

sections.heading: How to set it up so it sounds like you
paragraphs: The difference between an agent that books calls and one that annoys people is almost entirely in the setup. Start with the questions you already get every week and write down how you'd answer each one. Add your real prices or ranges, your service area, and the one or two things you need to know before you'd book someone.

Decide where the line is. Give it a clear rule for when to hand a conversation to you, and keep that rule tight at first. You can loosen it once you've read a few weeks of conversations and trust what it's saying.

Then connect it to your actual calendar, not a link it pastes into the chat. Asking someone to leave the conversation and fill out a form is where a lot of bookings fall apart. Offering two specific times right in the DM is what keeps them.
If you're wondering how this fits with the rest of your follow-up, like texts, calls, and missed leads from your ads, our [FAQ](/faq) walks through how the pieces work together.
The message at 9:40 on a Tuesday night is going to keep coming. The only question is whether someone answers it while that person is still deciding.
